notes.title: 1. About French
notes.content:
• French (le français) is spoken in France, Belgium, Switzerland, Canada (Quebec), many African countries
and more.
• It is a Romance language, descended from Latin, so many words look like English words (table,
important, restaurant).
• French has the same letters as English, plus accent marks that change sound or meaning.
• Every noun is either masculine or feminine. Words like “the”, “a” and adjectives change to match.
• Verbs change their ending depending on who is doing the action (je parle, tu parles, nous parlons).
• Many letters at the end of a word are not pronounced.
• Sentence order is mostly the same as English: subject + verb + rest (Je mange du pain = I eat bread).

notes.title: 2. Alphabet and sounds
notes.content:
Approximate English-style pronunciations are shown in the “Sounds like” column.
The alphabet (l’alphabet)
[TABLE]
Letter | Name | Letter | Name | Letter | Name
A | ah | J | zhee | S | ess
B | bay | K | kah | T | tay
C | say | L | ell | U | ü (lips rounded, say “ee”)
D | day | M | emm | V | vay
E | uh | N | enn | W | doo-bluh-vay
F | eff | O | oh | X | eeks
G | zhay | P | pay | Y | ee-grek
H | ahsh | Q | kü | Z | zed
I | ee | R | air (rolled at the back of the throat) |  | 
[/TABLE]
Accent marks (les accents)
[TABLE]
Mark | Name | Example | What it does
é | accent aigu | été (summer) | Sounds like “ay”
è | accent grave | mère (mother) | Sounds like “eh” in “bed”
ê | accent circonflexe | fête (party) | Sounds like “eh”; often marks a dropped “s” from older French
à, ù | accent grave | à (at/to), où (where) | Does not change the sound; separates words like ou (or) and où (where)
ç | cédille | français | Makes “c” sound like “s” before a, o, u
ë, ï | tréma | Noël | Tells you to pronounce the vowel separately
[/TABLE]
Vowel sounds
[TABLE]
Spelling | Sounds like | Example
a | “ah” | ami (friend) ah-mee
e (end of word) | usually silent | petite puh-teet
e (short word) | “uh” | le luh, je zhuh
i | “ee” | si see
o | “oh” | moto mo-toh
u | “ü” (say “ee” with rounded lips) | tu tü
ou | “oo” as in “food” | vous voo
oi | “wah” | moi mwah
ai, ei | “eh” | lait (milk) leh
au, eau | “oh” | eau (water) oh
eu, œu | “uh” with rounded lips | deux (two) duh
an, en | nasal “ahn” (do not pronounce the n) | enfant (child)
on | nasal “ohn” | bon (good)
in, ain, ein | nasal “an” as in “ant”, no n | pain (bread)
un | nasal “uhn” | un (one/a)
[/TABLE]
Consonant sounds
[TABLE]
Spelling | Sounds like | Example
ch | “sh” | chat (cat) sha
j | “zh” as in “measure” | jour (day) zhoor
g before e, i, y | “zh” | girafe zhee-raf
g before a, o, u | hard “g” | gare (station)
gn | “ny” as in “canyon” | montagne (mountain)
c before e, i, y | “s” | ceci (this)
c before a, o, u | “k” | café
qu | “k” | qui (who) kee
h | always silent | hôtel oh-tel
r | soft growl at the back of the throat | rouge (red)
th | “t” | thé (tea) tay
ph | “f” | photo
[/TABLE]
Silent letters and liaison
• Final consonants are often silent: petit (puh-tee), grand (grahn), vous (voo), trop (troh).
• The letters c, r, f, l at the end are often pronounced: sac, chef, avec, mal.
• Liaison: a normally silent final consonant is pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel: vous
avez sounds like “voo-zah-vay”; les amis sounds like “lay-zah-mee”.
• Elision: le, la, je, me, te, se, de, ne, que drop their vowel and use an apostrophe before a vowel or
silent h: l’ami, j’aime, l’hôtel.

notes.title: 3. Greetings and politeness
notes.content:
[TABLE]
French | Sounds like | Meaning
Bonjour | bohn-zhoor | Hello / Good morning / Good day
Bonsoir | bohn-swahr | Good evening (used after about 6 pm)
Bonne nuit | bun nwee | Good night (when going to bed)
Salut | sa-lü | Hi / Bye (informal, with friends)
Au revoir | oh ruh-vwahr | Goodbye
À bientôt | ah byan-toh | See you soon
À demain | ah duh-man | See you tomorrow
Merci | mehr-see | Thank you
Merci beaucoup | mehr-see boh-koo | Thank you very much
De rien | duh ryan | You’re welcome (literally “of nothing”)
S’il vous plaît | seel voo pleh | Please (formal or to several people)
S’il te plaît | seel tuh pleh | Please (informal, to one friend)
Excusez-moi | ex-kü-zay mwah | Excuse me
Pardon | par-dohn | Sorry / Pardon me
Désolé(e) | day-zo-lay | I’m sorry (add “e” if you are female)
Oui / Non | wee / nohn | Yes / No
D’accord | da-kor | OK / Agreed
Comment ça va ? | ko-mohn sa va | How are you? (informal)
Comment allez-vous ? | ko-mohn ta-lay voo | How are you? (formal)
Ça va bien | sa va byan | I’m fine / Things are going well
Pas mal | pah mal | Not bad
Comme ci, comme ça | kom see kom sa | So-so
Et vous ? / Et toi ? | ay voo / ay twah | And you? (formal / informal)
[/TABLE]
Tu or vous? Tu is for one friend, family member or child. Vous is for one person you do not know well,
someone older or in authority, and for any group.

notes.title: 4. Introducing yourself
notes.content:
[TABLE]
French | Meaning
Je m’appelle Manu. | My name is Manu.
Comment tu t’appelles ? | What is your name? (informal)
Comment vous appelez-vous ? | What is your name? (formal)
Enchanté(e). | Nice to meet you.
Je suis indien / indienne. | I am Indian (male / female).
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
French | Meaning
J’habite en Inde. | I live in India.
J’ai trente ans. | I am thirty years old (literally “I have thirty years”).
Je suis étudiant(e). | I am a student.
Je travaille dans un bureau. | I work in an office.
Je parle hindi et un peu français. | I speak Hindi and a little French.
Je ne comprends pas. | I don’t understand.
Parlez plus lentement, s’il vous plaît. | Please speak more slowly.
Comment dit-on … en français ? | How do you say … in French?
[/TABLE]
Word-by-word breakdown
Je m’appelle Manu.
[TABLE]
Je I | m’ myself | appelle call | Manu Manu
[/TABLE]
Literal meaning: “I call myself Manu.” This is how French says “My name is Manu.”
J’habite à Ajmer.
[TABLE]
J’ I (je, shortened) | habite live | à in / at | Ajmer Ajmer
[/TABLE]
Je suis étudiant et j’aime le français.
[TABLE]
Je I | suis am | étudiant student | et and | j’ I | aime like / love
le the | français French |  |  |  | 
[/TABLE]
Sample conversation
A: Bonjour ! Comment vous appelez-vous ?
Hello! What is your name?
B: Je m’appelle Priya. Et vous ?
My name is Priya. And you?
A: Je m’appelle Marc. Enchanté !
My name is Marc. Nice to meet you!
B: Enchantée. Comment allez-vous ?
Nice to meet you. How are you?
A: Je vais bien, merci. Au revoir !
I’m well, thank you. Goodbye!

notes.title: 5. Subject pronouns
notes.content:
A subject pronoun tells you who does the action.
[TABLE]
French | Meaning | Notes
je (j’) | I | Not capitalised unless it starts a sentence
tu | you (one person) | Informal
il | he / it (masculine) | 
elle | she / it (feminine) | 
on | one / we / people | Very common in speech for “we”; uses the same verb form as il/elle
nous | we | 
vous | you (formal, or more than one person) | 
ils | they (masculine or mixed group) | 
elles | they (all feminine) | 
[/TABLE]
Stressed pronouns (used after prepositions or for emphasis): moi (me), toi (you), lui (him), elle (her), nous
(us), vous (you), eux (them, m.), elles (them, f.). Example: Et toi ? = And you?

notes.title: 6. Nouns and articles
notes.content:
Gender
• Every noun is masculine (masculin) or feminine (féminin), including objects: le livre (the book, m.), la
table (the table, f.).
• Nouns for people usually follow natural gender: un frère (brother), une sœur (sister).
• Common feminine endings: -tion, -sion, -té, -ette, -ie, -ure, -e (la nation, la liberté).
• Common masculine endings: -ment, -age, -eau, -isme, -er, -oir (le gouvernement, le voyage).
• Always learn a noun together with its article.
Articles
[TABLE]
Type | Masculine | Feminine | Before vowel | Plural
Definite (the) | le | la | l’ | les
Indefinite (a / an / some) | un | une | un / une | des
Partitive (some, an amount of) | du | de la | de l’ | des
[/TABLE]
• le garçon (the boy), la fille (the girl), l’école (the school), les enfants (the children)
• un livre (a book), une maison (a house), des amis (some friends)
• Je mange du pain. = I eat (some) bread. Je bois de l’eau. = I drink (some) water.
• French needs an article almost always; English can leave it out (“I like music” = J’aime la musique).
Plurals
• Most nouns add -s (silent): un livre → des livres.
• Nouns ending in -s, -x, -z stay the same: un fils → des fils.
• Nouns ending in -au, -eau, -eu add -x: un gâteau → des gâteaux.
• Most nouns ending in -al change to -aux: un journal → des journaux.
• Irregular: un œil → des yeux (eye), madame → mesdames.
• The -s is not pronounced, so you hear the plural from the article: le livre vs les livres.

notes.title: 7. The two key verbs: être and avoir
notes.content:
[TABLE]
Pronoun | être (to be) | avoir (to have)
je / j’ | suis | ai
tu | es | as
il / elle / on | est | a
nous | sommes | avons
vous | êtes | avez
ils / elles | sont | ont
[/TABLE]
Using être
• Identity and description: Je suis Manu. Elle est grande. (She is tall.)
• Profession and nationality (no article): Il est médecin. (He is a doctor.)
• Place: Nous sommes à Paris.
Using avoir
• Possession: J’ai un frère. (I have a brother.)
• Age: Tu as quel âge ? (How old are you?) J’ai dix ans.
• Feelings with avoir: J’ai faim (I’m hungry), J’ai soif (I’m thirsty), J’ai froid (I’m cold), J’ai chaud (I’m
hot), J’ai peur (I’m afraid).
• Il y a = there is / there are (from avoir): Il y a un chat.

notes.title: 8. Regular verbs and common irregular verbs
notes.content:
Verbs ending in -er (the biggest group)
• Take the infinitive (parler = to speak), remove -er, then add the endings below.
[TABLE]
Pronoun | Ending | parler (to speak) | aimer (to like/love)
je | -e | parle | j’aime
tu | -es | parles | aimes
il / elle / on | -e | parle | aime
nous | -ons | parlons | aimons
vous | -ez | parlez | aimez
ils / elles | -ent (silent) | parlent | aiment
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
Verb | Meaning | Verb | Meaning
parler | to speak | manger | to eat
aimer | to like / love | travailler | to work
habiter | to live (reside) | étudier | to study
regarder | to watch / look at | écouter | to listen
chanter | to sing | danser | to dance
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
Verb | Meaning | Verb | Meaning
donner | to give | chercher | to look for
jouer | to play | acheter | to buy
[/TABLE]
• Spelling change: manger → nous mangeons (keeps the soft “g” sound).
• French has one present tense for both “I speak” and “I am speaking”: Je parle.
Verbs ending in -ir and -re (regular)
[TABLE]
Pronoun | finir (to finish) | vendre (to sell)
je | finis | vends
tu | finis | vends
il / elle / on | finit | vend
nous | finissons | vendons
vous | finissez | vendez
ils / elles | finissent | vendent
[/TABLE]
Very common irregular verbs
[TABLE]
Pronoun | aller (to go) | faire (to do / make) | pouvoir (can) | vouloir (to want)
je | vais | fais | peux | veux
tu | vas | fais | peux | veux
il / elle / on | va | fait | peut | veut
nous | allons | faisons | pouvons | voulons
vous | allez | faites | pouvez | voulez
ils / elles | vont | font | peuvent | veulent
[/TABLE]
• Je vais à l’école. = I go to school.
• Je vais manger. = I am going to eat (aller + infinitive = near future).
• Je veux un café. = I want a coffee. Je voudrais un café. = I would like a coffee (more polite).
• Il fait chaud. = It is hot (weather uses faire).

notes.title: 9. Saying “not”
notes.content:
• Wrap the verb with ne … pas: Je parle → Je ne parle pas (I don’t speak).
• Before a vowel: ne becomes n’: Je n’aime pas le café. (I don’t like coffee.)
• In fast speech, “ne” is often dropped: Je sais pas.
• After a negative, un / une / des / du / de la become de (d’): J’ai un frère → Je n’ai pas de frère.
[TABLE]
French | Meaning | Example
ne … pas | not | Il n’est pas ici. (He is not here.)
ne … jamais | never | Je ne mange jamais de viande.
ne … rien | nothing | Je ne comprends rien.
ne … plus | no more / no longer | Il n’habite plus ici.
[/TABLE]
[TABLE]
French | Meaning | Example
ne … personne | nobody | Je ne connais personne.
[/TABLE]

notes.title: 10. Asking questions
notes.content:
Three ways to ask a yes/no question
• Raise your voice: Tu parles français ? (most common in speech)
• Add est-ce que: Est-ce que tu parles français ?
• Swap verb and pronoun (formal): Parlez-vous français ?
Question words
[TABLE]
French | Meaning | Example
qui | who | Qui est-ce ? (Who is it?)
que / qu’est-ce que | what | Qu’est-ce que c’est ? (What is it?)
où | where | Où habites-tu ?
quand | when | Quand partez-vous ?
pourquoi | why | Pourquoi tu pleures ?
parce que | because | Parce que je suis fatigué.
comment | how | Comment ça va ?
combien | how much / how many | Combien ça coûte ?
quel / quelle | which / what | Quelle heure est-il ? (What time is it?)
[/TABLE]
C’est = it is / this is. Ce sont = these/those are. Qu’est-ce que c’est ? = What is that?

notes.title: 11. Numbers
notes.content:
[TABLE]
No. | French | No. | French | No. | French
0 | zéro | 7 | sept | 14 | quatorze
1 | un / une | 8 | huit | 15 | quinze
2 | deux | 9 | neuf | 16 | seize
3 | trois | 10 | dix | 17 | dix-sept
4 | quatre | 11 | onze | 18 | dix-huit
5 | cinq | 12 | douze | 19 | dix-neuf
6 | six | 13 | treize | 20 | vingt
[/TABLE]
Tens
[TABLE]
No. | French | No. | French
20 | vingt | 60 | soixante
30 | trente | 70 | soixante-dix (60 + 10)
40 | quarante | 80 | quatre-vingts (4 × 20)
50 | cinquante | 90 | quatre-vingt-dix (4 × 20 + 10)
[/TABLE]
• 21 = vingt et un, 22 = vingt-deux, 31 = trente et un, 71 = soixante et onze, 81 =
quatre-vingt-un.
• 100 = cent, 200 = deux cents, 1000 = mille, 1,000,000 = un million.
• Belgium and Switzerland use septante (70) and nonante (90).
Ordinal numbers
premier / première (1st), deuxième (2nd), troisième (3rd), quatrième (4th), cinquième (5th). From 2nd
onward, add -ième to the number.

notes.title: 12. Days, months, seasons and time
notes.content:
[TABLE]
Day | Meaning | Month | Meaning
lundi | Monday | janvier | January
mardi | Tuesday | février | February
mercredi | Wednesday | mars | March
jeudi | Thursday | avril | April
vendredi | Friday | mai | May
samedi | Saturday | juin | June
dimanche | Sunday | juillet | July
 |  | août | August
 |  | septembre | September
 |  | octobre | October
 |  | novembre | November
 |  | décembre | December
[/TABLE]
• Days and months are not capitalised in French. The week starts on Monday.
• Date format is day first: le 17 octobre. The first of the month is le premier: le 1er mai.
• Seasons: le printemps (spring), l’été (summer), l’automne (autumn), l’hiver (winter).
Telling time and time words
• Quelle heure est-il ? = What time is it?
• Il est trois heures. = It is three o’clock. Il est midi = noon. Il est minuit = midnight.
• et quart = quarter past; et demie = half past; moins le quart = quarter to.
• aujourd’hui (today), demain (tomorrow), hier (yesterday), maintenant (now), le matin (morning),
l’après-midi (afternoon), le soir (evening), la nuit (night).
• la semaine (week), le mois (month), l’an / l’année (year), le jour (day).

notes.title: 13. Everyday words
notes.content:
Family (la famille)
[TABLE]
French | Meaning | French | Meaning
le père / le papa | father / dad | la mère / la maman | mother / mom
le frère | brother | la sœur | sister
le fils | son | la fille | daughter / girl
le grand-père | grandfather | la grand-mère | grandmother
l’oncle | uncle | la tante | aunt
le mari | husband | la femme | wife / woman
l’ami / l’amie | friend (m. / f.) | l’enfant | child
[/TABLE]
Colours (les couleurs)
[TABLE]
French | Meaning | French | Meaning
rouge | red | bleu(e) | blue
vert(e) | green | jaune | yellow
noir(e) | black | blanc / blanche | white
gris(e) | grey | orange | orange
rose | pink | marron | brown
[/TABLE]
Food and drink (la nourriture)
[TABLE]
French | Meaning | French | Meaning
l’eau (f.) | water | le pain | bread
le lait | milk | le fromage | cheese
le café | coffee | le riz | rice
le thé | tea | la viande | meat
le jus | juice | le poisson | fish
la pomme | apple | l’œuf (m.) | egg
la banane | banana | le légume | vegetable
le petit déjeuner | breakfast | le déjeuner / le dîner | lunch / dinner
[/TABLE]
Places and things
[TABLE]
French | Meaning | French | Meaning
la maison | house | l’école (f.) | school
la ville | city / town | le bureau | office / desk
la rue | street | le magasin | shop
la gare | train station | l’hôpital (m.) | hospital
le livre | book | le stylo | pen
la voiture | car | le téléphone | phone
l’argent (m.) | money / silver | le travail | work
[/TABLE]
Body and feelings
la tête (head), la main (hand), le pied (foot), le visage (face), l’œil / les yeux (eye / eyes). Feelings:
content(e) (happy), triste (sad), fatigué(e) (tired), malade (sick).

notes.title: 14. Adjectives and possessives
notes.content:
Adjective agreement
• Adjectives match the noun in gender and number.
• Feminine: usually add -e: petit → petite, grand → grande.
• Plural: usually add -s: petits, petites.
• Adjectives ending in -e already: no change in feminine: rouge, jeune, triste.
• Most adjectives go after the noun: une voiture rouge (a red car).
• A few short, common ones go before: grand, petit, bon, beau, jeune, vieux, nouveau, joli: une
petite maison.
[TABLE]
Masculine | Feminine | Meaning
grand | grande | big / tall
petit | petite | small / short
bon | bonne | good
mauvais | mauvaise | bad
beau | belle | beautiful
nouveau | nouvelle | new
vieux | vieille | old
heureux | heureuse | happy
intéressant | intéressante | interesting
facile | facile | easy
difficile | difficile | difficult
[/TABLE]
Possessive adjectives (my, your, his…)
[TABLE]
Meaning | Masculine | Feminine | Plural
my | mon | ma | mes
your (tu) | ton | ta | tes
his / her / its | son | sa | ses
our | notre | notre | nos
your (vous) | votre | votre | vos
their | leur | leur | leurs
[/TABLE]
• The form depends on the thing owned, not the owner: son frère and sa sœur can both mean “his” or
“her”.
• Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel, use mon / ton / son: mon amie (my female friend).
Demonstratives (this, that)
ce (m.), cet (m. before vowel), cette (f.), ces (plural): ce livre, cet homme, cette maison, ces enfants.

notes.title: 15. Small words you need
notes.content:
[TABLE]
French | Meaning | French | Meaning
et | and | ou | or
mais | but | donc | so / therefore
avec | with | sans | without
dans | in / inside | sur | on
sous | under | devant / derrière | in front of / behind
à | at / to / in | de (d’) | of / from
en | in / by / to (countries) | pour | for
chez | at the home of | ici / là | here / there
très | very | trop | too much
beaucoup | a lot | un peu | a little
aussi | also / too | toujours | always
souvent | often | parfois | sometimes
pas du tout | not at all | peut-être | maybe
[/TABLE]
Contractions with à and de
• à + le = au, à + les = aux: Je vais au marché. (I go to the market.)
• de + le = du, de + les = des: le livre du professeur (the teacher’s book).
• à la and de la stay the same.
Useful survival phrases
• Je voudrais … = I would like …
• Où est la gare ? = Where is the station?
• Combien ça coûte ? = How much does it cost?
• L’addition, s’il vous plaît. = The bill, please.
• Je ne sais pas. = I don’t know.
• Pouvez-vous m’aider ? = Can you help me?
• Parlez-vous anglais ? = Do you speak English?
• Répétez, s’il vous plaît. = Please repeat.
